the binding energy of noble gases, hydrogen and nitrogen increases with increase in the size of the aromatic core and the presence of a cage effect.

the binding energies of noble gases, hydrogen and nitrogen with the noncovalent binding strategy to capture noble gases, hydrogen, and nitrogen is significantly higher than that of their parent molecules.
the fluorinated benzene core linked with methelane units show a steady and substantial increase in binding energy with an increase in the number number of aromatic rings.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the binding energy of the noble gas, H2 and the N2 complexes with the cyclophanyl receptor RIV and RVIH are 5–9‐fold higher in magnitude than that of benzene and hexafluorocyclohexane, respectively, which may be projected as the highest interaction energy range reported so far.
the binding energies for noble gas and H2 and N 2 are in the following order: RIV > RIVH > RIII > RII > RI.
a molecular design strategy to capture noble gases, H 2 and N 2 using a neutral carbon framework is described.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
a simple molecular design strategy can be adopted to develop receptor systems with significant interaction energy for the capture of noble gases, hydrogen and nitrogen.
the fluorination of benzene rings in the receptor systems increases binding energy of noble gases and hydrogen.
the binding energy (E _{int} ) of noble gases, hydrogen and nitrogen to the cage receptor R _{IV} is 4.9, 7.0, 6.5, 6.2, 8.6 and 8.2 kcal/mol for He, Ne, Ar, Kr, H _{2} and N _{2}, respectively.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the cage effect is not only limited to noble gases but can be exploited for the capture of small molecules such as H2 and N₂.

fluorination of the benzene rings and the introduction of a cyclophane structure in the host framework can lead to the formation of a stable cage effect which can be exploited to develop novel molecular systems for the enthapment of noble gases and other small molecules such as H2 and N 2.

the binding energies for the non‐covalent interactions of noble gases, hydrogen and nitrogen with a series of neutral carbon frameworks can be tuned by the introduction of fluorine atoms on the aromatic core of the receptor and by increasing the number of aromatic units.
